data.why: the repo ships no sample plate photos (static/uploads and labeller/data only contain .gitkeep placeholders), so a stock agar-plate image stands in for the plate photo a microbiologist would upload

goals: Upload a photo of an agar plate and get an automatic colony count instead of tallying by eye
Review the auto-detected colonies overlaid on the plate and click to add missed colonies or remove false positives before trusting the number
Get a usable count on a gridded counting plate, which defeats plain image-processing approaches
Recognize when a plate is too dense to count reliably (TNTC) and should be diluted and re-plated instead
Compare the trained-model engine against the classical computer-vision fallback on the same plate
Feed corrected counts back into the training dataset so the detector improves over time

review.summary: The tree covers the core human-in-the-loop loop well: upload, auto-detect, click to add or remove, resize, reset, save. The labels are clean, and most of the cited screens match their nodes. One causal claim is wrong: it credits Split with raising the count from 2 to 44, when sensitivity did it and Split has no effect on classical CV. The tree also skips the README's headline gridded-plate case, which works offline, and never reads off the final count, so it needs fixes before filing.
